notes.front: What is an Azure DevOps dashboard?
notes.back: A customisable, interactive signboard for a team or project that shows real-time information through configurable charts and widgets.
notes.explanation: Each dashboard is associated with a team or with a project.
notes.example: Like a pinned status page for the team, but built from widgets you choose and arrange.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Web portal data views and reports” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Dashboards**: Customizable interactive signboards that provide real-time information. Dashboards are associated with a team or a project and display configurable charts and widgets.

notes.front: What is a dashboard widget in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: An item that displays information and charts on a dashboard; many are configurable or scoped to a team or the signed-in user.
notes.explanation: Widgets draw their information from one or more data stores or charts kept within the system.
notes.example: Like a tile on a phone’s home screen, but showing, say, a build pipeline’s history on the team dashboard.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Widgets display information and charts on dashboards. Many widgets are configurable or scoped to a team or the logged-in user account. They display information from one or more data stores or charts maintained within the system.

notes.front: What is lead time in Azure Boards?
notes.back: The elapsed time from when a work item is created until it reaches a Completed state.
notes.explanation: It spans the item’s whole life from creation, and the guidance uses it to estimate delivery times.
notes.example: Like the time from ordering a meal to it reaching your table, not just the time the chef spends cooking.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Key definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Lead time — The elapsed time from when a work item is created until it reaches a Completed state. Use lead time to estimate delivery times and track SLAs.

notes.front: What is cycle time in Azure Boards?
notes.back: The elapsed time from when a work item first enters an In Progress state until it reaches a Completed state.
notes.explanation: It starts only when work begins, and the guidance uses it to find process bottlenecks and measure team efficiency.
notes.example: Like timing only the chef’s cooking, from the moment they pick up the order to plating it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Key definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Cycle time — The elapsed time from when a work item first enters an In Progress state until it reaches a Completed state. Use cycle time to identify process bottlenecks and measure team efficiency.

notes.front: What is a cumulative flow diagram (CFD)?
notes.back: A chart of the count of work items in each state or board column over time.
notes.explanation: Cycle time and lead time, its two primary metrics, are read off the chart.
notes.example: Like a stacked chart of how many orders sit in “received”, “cooking” and “served” each day.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Chart metrics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: CFDs show the count of work items grouped by state or column over time. The two primary metrics for tracking are cycle time and lead time. You extract these metrics from the chart.

notes.front: What does velocity track in Azure Boards?
notes.back: A team’s capacity to deliver work, sprint after sprint.
notes.explanation: The Velocity widget is configured with a team, a work item type, an aggregation field and a number of sprints.
notes.example: Like a runner’s lap times over a season, but counting the work a team finishes in each sprint.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog”, “Velocity” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Velocity widget tracks a team's capacity to deliver work sprint after sprint. You configure the widget by selecting a team, a work item type, an aggregation field, and the number of sprints.

notes.front: What is a sprint burndown in Azure Boards?
notes.back: A team’s burndown chart for one sprint, used to mitigate risk and check for scope creep during the sprint.
notes.explanation: The Analytics-based widget lets you choose the team, the iteration and the time period.
notes.example: Like a countdown of pages left to write before an essay deadline, but for a sprint’s remaining work.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog”, “Sprint Burndown (Analytics)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A team's burndown chart for a sprint to the dashboard. This widget is based on Analytics data. You have several configuration options for this widget, including selecting a team, iteration, and time period. Teams use the burndown chart to mitigate risk and check for scope creep throughout the sprint cycle.

notes.front: What is Analytics in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: The reporting platform for Azure DevOps, built for fast read access and server-based aggregations.
notes.explanation: It replaced the previous reporting platform, and being built for reporting is what makes it fast at aggregations.
notes.example: Like a reporting copy of a shop’s till data, tuned for totals and trends rather than for serving customers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Analytics is the reporting platform for Azure DevOps, replacing the previous platform based on SQL Server Reporting Services. Built specifically for reporting, Analytics is optimized for fast read-access and server-based aggregations.

notes.front: What is Power BI integration with Analytics?
notes.back: Importing Analytics data into Power BI, a suite of business analytics tools, through data connectors.
notes.explanation: The connectors are Analytics views, the OData query and the OData feed.
notes.example: Like exporting bank statements into a budgeting app, but the link stays live through a connector.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Power BI integration and data connectors” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: We provide multiple data connectors to support importing data into Power BI: ### Available connectors - **Analytics views**: Prefiltered, optimized data views - **OData query**: Direct query access for custom scenarios - **OData feed**: Real-time data streaming for live dashboards

notes.front: What are Analytics views?
notes.back: A web portal feature for filtering work tracking data, used to generate Power BI reports through a dedicated data connector.
notes.explanation: You can use default views or define custom ones for status and trend reports.
notes.example: Like a saved spreadsheet filter, but one that Power BI can read directly.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Analytics views” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Analytics views provide a web portal feature that supports filtering work tracking data for status and trend reports. With Analytics views, you can use default or custom views to generate reports in Power BI through a dedicated data connector.

notes.front: What are OData queries against Analytics?
notes.back: Queries in the Open Data Protocol that read Analytics metadata or data, even from a web browser, for programmatic access.
notes.explanation: Queries can read the Analytics metadata as well as the data itself.
notes.example: Like typing a search into an address bar, but the answer is Azure DevOps data in a structured form.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “OData queries and metadata access” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Analytics provides full accessibility through OData (Open Data Protocol). From a web browser, you can query the Analytics metadata or data using OData queries, enabling programmatic access to your Azure DevOps data.

notes.front: What is the pipeline pass rate report?
notes.back: A report of a pipeline’s pass rate and its trend over time, showing which task failures cause most failed runs.
notes.explanation: Knowing the top failing tasks tells you what to fix first.
notes.example: Like a league table of the players who concede most goals, but for tasks in failed pipeline runs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline pass rate report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Pipeline pass rate report provides a granular view of the pipeline pass rate and its trend over time. You can also view which specific task failure contributes to a high number of pipeline run failures, and use that insight to fix the top failing tasks.

notes.front: What is the pipeline duration report?
notes.back: A report of how long a pipeline typically takes to complete successfully, with its duration trend and top tasks by duration.
notes.explanation: The top tasks by duration show where to optimise the pipeline’s running time.
notes.example: Like a commute log that shows which stretch of road costs you the most minutes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline duration report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Pipeline duration report shows how long your pipeline typically takes to complete successfully. You can review the duration trend and analyze the top tasks by duration to optimize the duration of the pipeline.

notes.front: What is the test failures report?
notes.back: A detailed view of the top failing tests in a pipeline, with their failure details.
notes.explanation: Each top failing test comes with its failure details, not just a count.
notes.example: Like a list of the most-returned products in a shop, with the reason each came back.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Test failures report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Test failures report provides a granular view of the top failing tests in the pipeline, along with the failure details.

notes.front: What is Test Analytics in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: Near real-time visibility into test data for builds and releases.
notes.explanation: It improves pipeline efficiency by identifying repetitive, high-impact quality issues.
notes.example: Like a fitness tracker for your test suite, showing trends rather than a single day’s result.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Test Analytics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Test analytics provides near real-time visibility into your test data for builds and releases. It helps improve the efficiency of your pipeline by identifying repetitive, high impact quality issues.

notes.front: What are pipeline dashboard widgets?
notes.back: Widgets on team dashboards that show the status of build and release pipelines and test result trends.
notes.explanation: They bring pipeline health onto the same dashboard as the team’s other information.
notes.example: Like a departures board for your builds and releases, placed on the team’s dashboard.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Monitor your pipelines with dashboard widgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can monitor your pipelines by adding widgets to team dashboards in Azure DevOps. Widgets give you visibility to the status of your build and release pipelines and monitor test results trends.

notes.front: What do the code tile and build history widgets show?
notes.back: Activity in a repository or branch folder (code tiles) and a histogram of the builds run for a build pipeline (build history).
notes.explanation: Together they follow code activity, build progress and deployment status on one dashboard.
notes.example: Like a doorbell camera log for a repository folder, beside a bar chart of recent builds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Monitor code activity, build progress, and deployment status” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With the code tile widgets, you can monitor the activity occurring within a repository or branch folder. Build history displays a histogram of all builds run for a specific build pipeline.
introduces: code, build and release chart widgets
uses: code, build and release chart widgets

notes.front: What are manual testing progress and trend charts?
notes.back: Charts that track manual testing progress and results, built from a test plan rather than a query.
notes.explanation: Like work item query-based charts, you can add them to a dashboard.
notes.example: Like a query-based bug chart, but counting test cases ready to run or passing in each suite.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Charts: Manual testing progress, results, and trends” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The steps to creating charts that track manual testing progress and results are similar to the ones for tracking work. The starting point is the test plan rather than a query.
introduces: manual testing progress and trend charts
uses: manual testing progress and trend charts

notes.front: What are charts in GitHub Projects insights?
notes.back: Charts built from the items in a project, with filters, chart type and displayed information you choose.
notes.explanation: A chart you create is available to anyone who can view the project.
notes.example: Like a pivot chart over a spreadsheet, where the spreadsheet is your project’s issues and pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”
notes.evidence: When you create a chart, you set the filters, chart type, the information displayed, and the chart is available to anyone that can view the project. You can generate two types of chart: current charts and historical charts.

notes.front: What are GitHub Actions usage metrics?
notes.back: Metrics that track how many minutes your workflows and jobs consume.
notes.explanation: They help you understand the cost of running Actions and stay within your plan limits.
notes.example: Like an itemised phone bill, but listing Actions minutes by workflow, job and repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Actions metrics”, “About GitHub Actions metrics” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-actions-metrics.md)
notes.evidence: You can use this data to understand the cost of running Actions and ensure you're staying within your plan limits.

notes.front: What are GitHub Actions performance metrics?
notes.back: Metrics on the efficiency and reliability of workflows and jobs, such as run times, queue times and failure rates.
notes.explanation: They help identify bottlenecks, slow-running jobs or frequently failing workflows.
notes.example: Like a car’s trip computer showing journey times and breakdowns, not fuel costs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Actions metrics”, “About GitHub Actions metrics” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-actions-metrics.md)
notes.evidence: Performance metrics focus on the efficiency and reliability of your workflows and jobs. With performance metrics, you can monitor key indicators like job run times, queue times, and failure rates to identify bottlenecks, slow-running jobs, or frequently failing workflows.

notes.front: What do repository graphs on GitHub show?
notes.back: Information on a repository’s contributors and commits, and its forks and network, among other data.
notes.explanation: A maintainer can use them to understand who is using the repository and why.
notes.example: Like a website’s visitor statistics, but for a repository’s contributors, commits and forks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About repository graphs”
notes.evidence: contributors and commits to the repository, and a repository's forks and network. If you maintain a repository, you can use this data to get a better understanding of who's using your repository and why they're using it.

notes.front: What does the security overview in GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps provide?
notes.back: Insight into your organisation’s level of risk and security protection.
notes.explanation: It comes with both Secret Protection and Code Security for Azure DevOps.
notes.example: Like a building’s alarm panel showing which doors are armed, but for repositories’ security findings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Security overview, which provides insight into your organization's level of risk and security protection Code Security includes the following features:
introduces: security overview for GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps
uses: security overview for GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: Which Application Insights tools give operations metrics for continuous monitoring?
notes.back: Monitoring tools such as alerts, metrics and logs, which track an application’s health and set up proactive notifications.
notes.explanation: Metrics, for instance, let you dig into usage patterns and trends.
notes.example: Like a car’s dashboard warning lights and gauges, but for a running web application.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to Application Insights - OpenTelemetry observability”, “Monitoring” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-monitor-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use these tools to continuously track your application's health and set up proactive notifications. * Alerts: Monitor a wide range of aspects of your application and trigger various actions. * Metrics: Dive deep into metrics data to understand usage patterns and trends.

notes.front: What are DORA metrics?
notes.back: DevOps Research and Assessment metrics: a set of metrics that measure software delivery performance.
notes.explanation: The source counts DORA among the standard metrics, and lead time, deployment frequency, mean time to restore and change failure rate are among the measures it names.
notes.example: Like judging a kitchen by how quickly and how often dishes reach the pass and how many are sent back, not by how busy the cooks look.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Foundations of Platform Engineering”, “Platform Engineering Capability Model”, “Measurements and Feedback” (MicrosoftDocs/learn on GitHub)
notes.evidence: standard metrics like DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment is a set of metrics that measure software delivery performance, including lead time, deployment frequency, mean time to restore, and change failure rate)

notes.front: What are two things a team can use its Azure DevOps dashboards for?
notes.back: Sharing information; viewing status, progress and trends; accessing quick links (any two).
notes.explanation: Each team can add and configure several dashboards for these purposes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Configurable dashboards” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Each team can add and configure multiple dashboards to: - Share information. - View status, progress, and trends. - Access quick links and other functions.

notes.front: Can a user with Stakeholder access create and edit Azure DevOps dashboards?
notes.back: No: Stakeholders can view dashboards, but creating and editing them needs Basic access.
notes.explanation: In the access-level table, creating and editing dashboards is ticked for Basic but not for Stakeholder.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Supported features for access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Dashboards (Create and edit) :::column-end::: :::column span="1"::: :::column-end::: :::column span="1"::: ✔️

notes.front: Besides the widget catalog, where can dashboard widgets come from?
notes.back: The Marketplace, or your own widget built with the `REST API`.
notes.explanation: The out-of-box catalog is only the starting set.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Marketplace widgets and extensibility” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In addition to the widgets available in the widget catalog, you might find interesting widgets in the Marketplace. Or, you can create your own widget by using the REST API.

notes.front: Which two widgets does the widget catalog list under Repos?
notes.back: Code Tile and Pull Request.
notes.explanation: The catalog groups its out-of-box widgets by the service they support.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog”, “Supported OOB widgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Repos | - Code Tile (Repository, Branch, Folder)
- Pull Request (Team)

notes.front: Under which service does the widget catalog list the Test Results Trend widget?
notes.back: Test Plans.
notes.explanation: Test Plans also holds Chart for Test Plans and Test Results Trend (Advanced).
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog”, “Supported OOB widgets” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence:
Test Plans | - Chart for Test Plans
- Test Results Trend (Build, Release)
- Test Results Trend (Advanced) (Analytics, Build, Release)

notes.front: According to the widget guidance, what is lead time used to estimate?
notes.back: Delivery times.
notes.explanation: Lead time runs from the item’s creation until it reaches a Completed state.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Key definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The elapsed time from when a work item is created until it reaches a Completed state. Use lead time to estimate delivery times

notes.front: What are two uses of cycle time, according to the widget guidance?
notes.back: Identifying process bottlenecks and measuring team efficiency.
notes.explanation: Cycle time is measured only from when a work item first enters an In Progress state.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Key definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Cycle time — The elapsed time from when a work item first enters an In Progress state until it reaches a Completed state. Use cycle time to identify process bottlenecks and measure team efficiency.

notes.front: In the Cycle Time or Lead Time widget, which Time period setting suits continuous flow?
notes.back: Rolling period, with a number of days.
notes.explanation: Start date gives a fixed scope view instead, useful for Scrumban or standard sprint processes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Configure the Cycle Time or Lead Time widget” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Choose Rolling period for continuous flow (specify the number of days), or Start date for a fixed scope view (useful for Scrumban or standard sprint processes).

notes.front: What must a team do for its Lead Time and Cycle Time charts to give useful data?
notes.back: Update work item status quickly as work progresses.
notes.explanation: The charts’ data is only as current as the work item status the team records.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Configure the Cycle Time or Lead Time widget” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For your charts to provide useful data, your team needs to quickly update work item status as work progresses.

notes.front: A Cycle Time chart shows the last 30 days. How many previous days does its daily moving average use?
notes.back: Five: 20 per cent of 30 is 6, rounded down to the nearest odd number.
notes.explanation: N is always 20 per cent of the days shown, rounded down to the nearest odd number.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Moving average and standard deviation calculations” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: N is 20 percent of the number of days the chart shows, rounded down to the nearest odd number. - Example: If the chart shows the last 30 days, then N = 5 days (20 percent of 30 days is 6, rounded down to 5).

notes.front: On a Lead Time or Cycle Time chart, the shaded band around the trend line shows the {{c1::standard deviation}}.
notes.explanation: It marks the range of typical variation around the moving average.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Summary elements” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The shaded band around the trend line shows the standard deviation — the range of typical variation.

notes.front: Does the built-in CFD give discrete lead time and cycle time values?
notes.back: No; the Lead Time and Cycle Time widgets provide those values.
notes.explanation: Neither the Analytics CFD widget nor the CFD on a backlog or board gives discrete values.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Chart metrics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The CFD widget that uses Analytics data and the built-in CFD that you can view from a team backlog or board don't provide discrete lead time and cycle time values. However, the Lead Time and Cycle Time widgets do provide these values.

notes.front: How does work in progress relate to cycle and lead times?
notes.back: More work in progress leads to longer cycle and lead times; less leads to shorter ones.
notes.explanation: That correlation is a key reason to set work-in-progress limits on the board.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Chart metrics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: More WIP leads to longer cycle times and longer lead times. The opposite is also true—less WIP leads to shorter cycle and lead times. When the development team focuses on fewer items, they reduce cycle and lead times. This correlation is a key reason to set WIP limits

notes.front: What is the guidance’s rule of thumb for work in progress per team member?
notes.back: No more than two items in progress at any given time.
notes.explanation: The limit is two rather than stricter because reality frequently intrudes on software development.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Is there too much WIP?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: There should be no more than two items in progress per team member at any given time. The main reason for using a limit of two items, not a stricter limit, is that reality frequently intrudes on the software development process.

notes.front: Can one Velocity widget track several teams together?
notes.back: No; it tracks the velocity of a single team.
notes.explanation: The widget uses Analytics data and is configured per team.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog”, “Velocity” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The widget takes advantage of Analytics data. You can track the velocity for a single team, not multiple teams.

notes.front: Is Analytics a real-time store?
notes.back: No; a change can take up to 30 seconds to show up in Analytics.
notes.explanation: Analytics queries a copy of the Azure DevOps data, and copying introduces the delay.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Data latency” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Because the data is copied, Analytics is **not a real-time store**. Copying the data introduces up to a 30-second delay before the data associated with any one change shows up in Analytics.

notes.front: When is an Analytics query response paged?
notes.back: When it exceeds 10,000 results.
notes.explanation: With the recommended query patterns, Analytics answers queries within 3 to 5 seconds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Query performance” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Analytics responds to any aggregation or non-aggregated query within 3 to 5 seconds. The query response is paged if it exceeds 10,000 results.

notes.front: What does defining an Analytics view save you when building several reports?
notes.back: Defining the same filters again: you define them once and reuse them.
notes.explanation: Pre-filtered data also means less data transfer and faster report loading.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Benefits of Analytics views” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Pre-filtered data**: Define filters once and reuse across multiple reports - **Performance optimization**: Reduced data transfer and faster report loading

notes.front: Where do you open the Cumulative Flow Diagram and team Velocity reports in Azure Boards?
notes.back: On the Analytics tab of the backlog or board.
notes.explanation: These in-context reports derive from Analytics data.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “In-context reports: Work tracking” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Boards provides several in-context reports that derive from Analytics data. From your backlog or board, you can view the Cumulative Flow Diagram and team Velocity reports by selecting the Analytics tab.

notes.front: By default, how many days of data do Azure Pipelines reports show, and what else can you filter them by?
notes.back: The last 14 days; you can change the date range or filter by branch.
notes.explanation: The branch filter shows the report for one branch or a set of branches.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Filters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Pipelines reports can be further filtered by date range or branch. - **Date range**: The default view shows data from the last 14 days. The filter helps change this range.

notes.front: With which service is Test Analytics currently available?
notes.back: Only with Azure Pipelines.
notes.explanation: Test results produced outside Azure Pipelines are not covered.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Test Analytics” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Test analytics is currently available only with Azure Pipelines.

notes.front: In the Build History widget, what does a yellow bar mean?
notes.back: The build completed without tests.
notes.explanation: Green means completed and red means failed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Out Of Box widget catalog”, “Build History” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Bar color indicates: green-completed, red-failed, and yellow-completed without tests.

notes.front: Which chart types can a query-based status chart use?
notes.back: Pie, bar, column, stacked bar and pivot.
notes.explanation: Trend charts use stacked area, line and area instead.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Charts: Work tracking status and trends” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Status charts include pie, bar, column, stacked bar, and pivot. Trend charts include stacked area, line, and area.

notes.front: Is there a chart or widget that tracks changes to sprint scope?
notes.back: No; you find items added to or moved out of a sprint with the Query Editor.
notes.explanation: The Query Editor, not a dashboard chart, is the tool for finding these items.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Sprint scope change” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: There's no chart or widget that tracks changes to sprint scope. However, you can determine work items added to a sprint or moved out of a sprint by using the Query Editor.

notes.front: How can an organisation owner let someone view GitHub Actions usage metrics without making them an owner?
notes.back: Give them a custom organisation role with the “View organization Actions metrics” permission.
notes.explanation: The permission is selected when the custom organisation role is created.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Actions metrics”, “Enabling access to GitHub Actions metrics” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/enabling-actions-metrics.md)
notes.evidence: To provide users with access, select the "View organization Actions metrics" role when creating a custom organization role.

notes.front: Where is GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps available?
notes.back: Only in Azure DevOps Services, and only for Git repositories.
notes.explanation: It is not offered for other kinds of repository or for Azure DevOps Server.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps is only available for Azure DevOps Services and specifically for code Git repositories.
uses: security overview for GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps

notes.front: DORA metrics measure software delivery performance; they include lead time, deployment frequency, {{c1::mean time to restore}} and change failure rate.
notes.explanation: Alongside measures of speed such as lead time and deployment frequency, the set names how long restoring takes and how often changes fail.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, “Foundations of Platform Engineering”, “Platform Engineering Capability Model”, “Measurements and Feedback” (MicrosoftDocs/learn on GitHub)
notes.evidence: standard metrics like DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment is a set of metrics that measure software delivery performance, including lead time, deployment frequency, mean time to restore, and change failure rate)

notes.front: A customer asks how long, on average, their requests take from the moment they are logged until they are done. Which metric answers that?
notes.back: C) Lead time.
notes.choices:
A) Velocity
B) Cycle time
C) Lead time
D) Pipeline duration
notes.choicesExplained: B: cycle time starts only when work begins, not when the item is created. A: velocity tracks how much a team delivers per sprint. D: pipeline duration measures how long a pipeline run takes.
notes.explanation: Lead time runs from the work item’s creation until it reaches a Completed state.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Key definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Lead time — The elapsed time from when a work item is created until it reaches a Completed state. Use lead time to estimate delivery times

notes.front: A team lead wants to find where work slows down once developers have started on it. Which metric suits that best?
notes.back: C) Cycle time.
notes.choices:
A) Lead time
B) Sprint burndown
C) Cycle time
D) Pipeline pass rate
notes.choicesExplained: A: lead time also counts the time before work starts. B: a sprint burndown shows remaining work in a sprint. D: pass rate measures pipeline failures, not work items.
notes.explanation: Cycle time starts when work first enters In Progress, and the guidance uses it to identify process bottlenecks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Key definitions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Cycle time — The elapsed time from when a work item first enters an In Progress state until it reaches a Completed state. Use cycle time to identify process bottlenecks and measure team efficiency.

notes.front: On your team’s CFD, the In Progress band has swollen into a growing vertical oval over several weeks. What does that most likely show?
notes.back: D) Too much work in progress, lengthening cycle and lead times.
notes.choices:
A) A scope change in the sprint
B) Work is flowing evenly
C) The team has stopped updating work item status
D) Too much work in progress, lengthening cycle and lead times
notes.choicesExplained: A: scope changes show on the top line of a fixed-period CFD. C: missed status updates show as flat lines. B: even flow shows bands of similar, steady spacing.
notes.explanation: A large amount of work in progress usually shows as a vertical bulge, and the longer it lasts the more it becomes an oval.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Is there too much WIP?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A large amount of WIP usually shows up as a vertical bulge. The longer that there's a large amount of WIP, the more the bulge expands into an oval shape. This behavior is an indication that the WIP is negatively affecting the cycle and lead time.

notes.front: Work piles up in the Development column of a CFD while testing takes a long time. Where does the guidance say the problem most likely is?
notes.back: D) In a later step, such as testing, not necessarily in Development.
notes.choices:
A) In Development, where the bulge is
B) In the backlog, before Development
C) Nowhere: bulges are normal
D) In a later step, such as testing, not necessarily in Development
notes.choicesExplained: A: a bulge doesn’t necessarily mean the step where it shows is at fault. B: the guidance points to a succeeding step, not an earlier one. C: bulges come from work building up in one part of the system.
notes.explanation: Bulges indicate that a succeeding step has the problem, not necessarily the step where the bulge appears.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “How is the flow of work progressing?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For example, a bulge can occur when testing takes a long time but development takes less time. The result is that work accumulates in the development state. Bulges indicate that a succeeding step is having a problem, not necessarily the step in which the bulge is occurring.

notes.front: On one sprint day, three work items were added and three removed, and the fixed-period CFD’s top line stayed flat. How can you still track that scope change?
notes.back: A) Use the sprint burndown to monitor scope changes.
notes.choices:
A) Use the sprint burndown to monitor scope changes
B) Check the Velocity widget
C) Read it from the CFD top line
D) Check the pipeline pass rate report
notes.choicesExplained: C: the top line stays flat when equal numbers are added and removed on one day. B: velocity tracks delivery across sprints. D: the pass rate report is about pipeline runs.
notes.explanation: The guidance lists the sprint burndown among the ways to track scope changes a CFD cannot show.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Did the scope change?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: That scenario occurs when the same number of work items are added and removed on the same day. The line stays flat in this case. To track scope changes in this case, take the following actions: - Compare several charts with one another. - Monitor specific issues. - Use sprint burndown to monitor scope changes.

notes.front: You close a work item and immediately refresh an Analytics-based report, but the change is missing. What is the likeliest explanation?
notes.back: C) Analytics copies data, so a change can take up to 30 seconds to appear.
notes.choices:
A) Closed work items are never included in Analytics
B) Analytics only refreshes once a day
C) Analytics copies data, so a change can take up to 30 seconds to appear
D) The report needs Power BI to show new data
notes.choicesExplained: B: the delay is up to 30 seconds, not a day. A: Analytics is populated with all available Azure DevOps data and keeps updating. D: in-context and widget reports read Analytics directly.
notes.explanation: Analytics is not a real-time store; copying introduces a delay of up to 30 seconds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Data latency” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Because the data is copied, Analytics is **not a real-time store**. Copying the data introduces up to a 30-second delay before the data associated with any one change shows up in Analytics.

notes.front: Your pipeline fails often, and you want to know which tasks cause most of the failed runs. Which report do you open?
notes.back: B) The pipeline pass rate report.
notes.choices:
A) The pipeline duration report
B) The pipeline pass rate report
C) The cumulative flow diagram
D) Repository graphs
notes.choicesExplained: A: the duration report shows how long runs take and the slowest tasks. C: a CFD counts work items by state. D: repository graphs show contributors, commits, forks and traffic.
notes.explanation: The pass rate report shows which task failures contribute most to failed runs, so you can fix the top failing tasks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline pass rate report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can also view which specific task failure contributes to a high number of pipeline run failures, and use that insight to fix the top failing tasks.

notes.front: Successful runs of your pipeline have crept from 12 to 25 minutes. Which report shows the trend and the tasks taking longest?
notes.back: A) The pipeline duration report.
notes.choices:
A) The pipeline duration report
B) The pipeline pass rate report
C) Velocity
D) The test failures report
notes.choicesExplained: D: the test failures report lists the top failing tests. B: the pass rate report tracks failures, not run time. C: velocity measures work delivered per sprint.
notes.explanation: The duration trend confirms the slowdown, and the top tasks by duration show where the extra time goes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline duration report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Pipeline duration report shows how long your pipeline typically takes to complete successfully. You can review the duration trend and analyze the top tasks by duration to optimize the duration of the pipeline.

notes.front: Some tests fail only now and then, and a single run tells you nothing. Where do you look for the pattern?
notes.back: B) Test Analytics, watching the tests’ execution trends over a period.
notes.choices:
A) The pipeline duration report
B) Test Analytics, watching the tests’ execution trends over a period
C) The Development section of a work item
D) A default email subscription
notes.choicesExplained: A: the duration report is about run time. C: the Development section lists linked code and builds. D: a subscription notifies you of events but shows no trends.
notes.explanation: For nondeterministic tests, trends over a period help infer hidden patterns that one execution cannot show.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Test Analytics”, “Infer hidden patterns” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Looking at an individual instance of test execution might not provide any meaningful insights into the behavior. However, observing test execution trends for a period can help infer hidden patterns, and help you resolve the failures.
uses: Development section of a work item

notes.front: Several Power BI reports need the same filtered set of work tracking data. What should you define?
notes.back: A) An Analytics view.
notes.choices:
A) An Analytics view
B) A dashboard for each report
C) A Query Tile widget
D) A custom service hook subscription
notes.choicesExplained: B: dashboards display widgets; they don’t filter data for Power BI. C: a Query Tile summarises one shared query on a dashboard. D: service hooks send notifications to other services.
notes.explanation: An Analytics view lets you define the filters once and reuse them across reports.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Analytics?”, “Benefits of Analytics views” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Pre-filtered data**: Define filters once and reuse across multiple reports

notes.front: A manager with Stakeholder access wants to build a new dashboard for the team. What do they need?
notes.back: B) Basic access.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more: Stakeholders can create dashboards
B) Basic access
C) Membership of the Project Collection Administrators group
D) A Power BI licence
notes.choicesExplained: A: Stakeholders can view dashboards but not create or edit them. C: creating a dashboard is an access-level matter here, not an administrator role. D: dashboards are a web portal feature, not Power BI.
notes.explanation: Creating and editing dashboards is ticked for Basic access, not for Stakeholder.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Supported features for access levels” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Users with Stakeholder access get restricted privileges, granting them access to only those features outlined in the following table.

notes.front: You want a pie chart of active bugs by priority on the team dashboard. What is the sequence?
notes.back: B) Build a work item query, create a chart from it, then add the chart to the dashboard.
notes.choices:
A) Add a Velocity widget, then filter it to bugs
B) Build a work item query, create a chart from it, then add the chart to the dashboard
C) Open the CFD and switch it to a pie chart
D) Create a test plan, then chart its suites
notes.choicesExplained: A: velocity tracks delivery per sprint, not a breakdown of bugs. D: test plans are the starting point for test charts, not work item charts. C: a CFD is a flow chart over time, not a query-based status chart.
notes.explanation: Query-based charts start from a shared work item query, then go on the dashboard.
notes.source: Microsoft, “About dashboards, charts, reports, and widgets”, “Charts: Work tracking status and trends” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can open a shared query, create a chart, and add it to the dashboard.

notes.front: On a GitHub project, you want to see how completed and open work has changed over the last month. What kind of insights chart do you create?
notes.back: C) A historical chart, with the X-axis set to Time.
notes.choices:
A) A current chart grouped by assignee
B) A repository graph
C) A historical chart, with the X-axis set to Time
D) A GitHub Actions usage metrics view
notes.choicesExplained: A: current charts show the project’s items as they are now. B: repository graphs cover commits, contributors and traffic, not project items. D: usage metrics track Actions minutes.
notes.explanation: Historical charts track changes to the state of project items over time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About historical charts”
notes.evidence: You can create historical charts to visualize your project items over time. Historical charts track changes to the state of your project items.

notes.front: Jobs in your organisation seem to wait a long time before they start running. Which GitHub metrics show that?
notes.back: D) GitHub Actions performance metrics.
notes.choices:
A) Charts in GitHub Projects insights
B) GitHub Actions usage metrics
C) Repository graphs
D) GitHub Actions performance metrics
notes.choicesExplained: B: usage metrics track the minutes consumed. C: repository graphs cover contributors, commits, forks and traffic. A: Projects charts are built from project items.
notes.explanation: Performance metrics monitor indicators such as job run times, queue times and failure rates.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Actions metrics”, “About GitHub Actions metrics” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-actions-metrics.md)
notes.evidence: With performance metrics, you can monitor key indicators like job run times, queue times, and failure rates to identify bottlenecks, slow-running jobs, or frequently failing workflows.

notes.front: A Scrum team wants its Cycle Time widget to show a fixed scope matching each sprint. Which Time period setting should it choose?
notes.back: B) Start date.
notes.choices:
A) Rolling period
B) Start date
C) Field criteria
D) Swimlane
notes.choicesExplained: A: a rolling period suits continuous flow. C: field criteria filter work items by field values. D: a swimlane narrows the work items, not the time period.
notes.explanation: Start date gives a fixed scope view, useful for Scrumban or standard sprint processes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure lead time and cycle time widgets”, “Configure the Cycle Time or Lead Time widget” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Choose Rolling period for continuous flow (specify the number of days), or Start date for a fixed scope view (useful for Scrumban or standard sprint processes).

notes.front: Where do lead time and cycle time each start and end?
notes.back: Lead time: from creation to a Completed state. Cycle time: from entering In Progress or Resolved to a Completed state.
notes.explanation: Both end at Completed; only their start points differ.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “Lead time versus cycle time” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Lead time starts when a work item is created and ends when the work item enters a Completed state category. Cycle time starts when a work item enters an In Progress or Resolved state category and ends when it enters a Completed state category.

notes.front: How do current charts and historical charts in GitHub Projects insights differ?
notes.back: Current charts show project items as they are now; historical charts show changes to their state over time.
notes.explanation: Only historical charts follow changes to the items’ state.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About insights for Projects”, “About historical charts”
notes.evidence: You can create historical charts to visualize your project items over time. Historical charts track changes to the state of your project items.

notes.front: How do GitHub Actions usage metrics differ from performance metrics?
notes.back: Usage metrics track the minutes workflows and jobs consume; performance metrics track their efficiency and reliability.
notes.explanation: Usage data helps you understand the cost of running Actions; performance data is about how efficiently and reliably things run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Actions metrics”, “About GitHub Actions metrics” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-actions-metrics.md)
notes.evidence: You can use this data to understand the cost of running Actions and ensure you're staying within your plan limits. This is especially useful for identifying high-usage workflows or repositories. * **{% data variables.product.prodname_actions %} performance metrics:** Performance metrics focus on the efficiency and reliability of your workflows and jobs.

notes.front: On a CFD, how does a flat line differ from a bulge in how much of the system has the problem?
notes.back: Flat lines appear across many parts of the system; a bulge appears when only one or two parts have problems.
notes.explanation: Flat lines can come from work across one or more processes taking longer than planned.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Cumulative flow guidance for lead time and cycle time”, “How is the flow of work progressing?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Flat lines can also appear when the work across one or more processes takes longer than planned. Flat lines appear across many parts of the system because if only one or two parts have problems, you see a bulge.
